newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt says Israel, not PLO, must make concessions.
newsitem.headline: Egypt says Israel, not PLO, must make concessions.

text.p: Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, said on Saturday Israel must make concessions in peace talks before telling Palestinians to abandon their demands, rejecting the U.S. view of the dispute.

The comment followed a statement by U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher on Thursday that Israel had made moves toward clinching a deal on a partial withdrawal from the occupied West Bank city of Hebron and it was time for Palestinians to reciprocate.

"If there are any concession made by Israel, we would like to know them," Mubarak told reporters a day after his talks with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat. "Arafat was here and I did not understand from him that there were any concessions".

"Israel says they have made concessions and the Palestinians must do so," Mubarak said of Christopher's comments. "What can the Palestinians concede? They don't have anything. Does Israel want them to concede their dignity, their land, the right to protect their people?"
There has been no visible progress in Israeli-Palestinian talks on implementing a partial Israeli troop withdrawal from Hebron under an accord signed more than a year ago.
The United States dispatched Middle East mediator Dennis Ross to Israel on Saturday to revive peace talks, but Arafat warned in advance that he should not come as an advocate of Israeli positions.
Arabs have criticised the rightwing government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for trying to change the Hebron deal since it ousted the previous Labour government in May elections.
"There has been no progress whatsoever on the Hebron deal," Mubarak told a joint news conference with visiting Greek President Costis Stephanopoulos.

"All the Israelis are doing is changing some phrases but the same issues are still pending. A date has not even been set for the redeployment. If the Palestinians want to make concessions, then it's up to them," he added.

Israel demands better security for 400 Jewish settlers living among 100,000 Arabs in Hebron before it redeploys its troops. The Palestinians have rejected the proposed measures, which they have likened to apartheid.

Hebron is the last of seven towns in the West Bank due to be handed over to PLO self-rule under the 1995 agreement. Israel is also supposed to hand over more West Bank land to the PLO under signed peace deals but Palestinians fear Netanyahu will renege on them.

The United States, sponsor of the Israeli-Arab peace talks launched in 1991, has pressed Israelis and Palestinians to finalise an accord on Hebron and move on to negotiations on a final comprehensive peace deal.
But on Friday, after the comments by Christopher that were warmly welcomed by Israel, Arafat told reporters he saw nothing to suggest agreement on Hebron was possible.
"There's no sign of hope that in the future a solution will be reached that satisfies the Palestinian side, especially in view of the Israeli government's intransigence," he said.
Stephanopolous, who arrived on Friday for a three-day visit, told reporters Greece would lobby other European Union members for a more active political role in the peace process.
"The European Union can play a vital role in the Middle East peace process and Greece will push the EU to take a political role in this issue that matches its economic role," he said.
